word:greek-nt:G0071.explanation: Ago means to lead. It can also mean to bring a person, as when people are brought before governors and kings.

word:greek-nt:G0093.explanation: Adikia means injustice. It also means unrighteousness.

word:greek-nt:G0277.explanation: This word means “immovable” or “not moveable.” It describes someone or something that remains firmly in place rather than being shifted, displaced, or turned aside. As an adjective, it characterizes steadfastness and stability, whether literally or in a broader sense. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Corinthians 15:58; the surrounding verse is needed to understand its specific application there.

word:greek-nt:G0318.explanation: Anankē means necessity, a requirement that may be laid upon someone.

word:greek-nt:G0354.explanation: This word refers to an ascension or a taking up. It describes movement upward, especially the act of being taken up from one place or state to another. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, at Luke 9:51, so its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. Its central meaning remains the idea of ascent or removal upward, rather than a general reference to ordinary travel or movement.

word:greek-nt:G0466.explanation: Antanaplēroō means to fill up what is lacking—to complete or supply what is needed.

word:greek-nt:G0488.explanation: Antimetreo means to measure in return, giving an equivalent measure.

word:greek-nt:G0563.explanation: Aperispastōs means without distraction. It describes giving undivided attention rather than being pulled away.

word:greek-nt:G0602.explanation: Apokalypsis means an unveiling or revelation.

word:greek-nt:G0857.explanation: Apheidia means severity or severe treatment.

word:greek-nt:G0905.explanation: Ballantion means a purse or money-bag.

word:greek-nt:G0949.explanation: Bebaios means firm or steadfast. It can also describe something sure or certain.

word:greek-nt:G0970.explanation: This word means “force”: strength or pressure exerted to move, restrain, or overcome something. It points to power actively applied rather than merely possessed. The word occurs three times in the Greek New Testament, all in Acts, so its recorded use is limited to that corpus and book. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the central idea is exerted strength or compulsion.

word:greek-nt:G1003.explanation: Boaz is a personal name: it identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek New Testament, the word is rendered “Boaz” and occurs three times across two verses, appearing in Matthew 1:5 and Luke 3:32. Its function is therefore to identify the person named Boaz, not to express a general concept, command, or character trait.

word:greek-nt:G1238.explanation: Diadema means a crown or diadem.

word:greek-nt:G1274.explanation: Dianyo means to finish, complete, or accomplish fully. It is used for finishing a journey.

word:greek-nt:G1380.explanation: Dokeo means to think. It can also mean to seem or appear.

word:greek-nt:G1551.explanation: Ekdechomai means to wait for or expect. It can describe waiting for others and expecting someone to come.

word:greek-nt:G1616.explanation: This word means “earnestness,” expressing serious, sincere, and wholehearted commitment. It describes an attitude marked by genuine zeal rather than casual interest or weak effort. In the Greek New Testament, it appears once, in Acts 26:7. Because the word is presented without broader contextual evidence here, its central sense is best kept focused on the quality of earnest devotion or purposeful concern it names. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself points to seriousness and wholehearted intent.

word:greek-nt:G1735.explanation: This word means “be possible” or “it is possible.” It expresses that something can happen or may be the case, rather than declaring that it certainly will happen. In a sentence, it functions as a statement about possibility or what may be permitted by circumstances. It appears once in the Greek New Testament, in Luke 13:33. Its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic sense remains the affirmation that something is possible.

word:greek-nt:G1740.explanation: Endoxazomai means to be glorified—to be recognized as glorious.

word:greek-nt:G1779.explanation: Entaphiazo means to prepare someone for burial. It can also mean to embalm.

word:greek-nt:G1814.explanation: Exallomai means to leap up or jump up.

word:greek-nt:G1858.explanation: This Greek New Testament verb means “to celebrate a festival” or “to keep a festival.” It describes taking part in a festival observance rather than merely recognizing a special day. The word appears once in the Greek New Testament, in 1 Corinthians 5:8. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense is active participation in a festival or feast. Both approved meanings point to observing such a celebration as an ongoing or deliberate action.

word:greek-nt:G1999.explanation: ἐπίστασιν means a gathering or tumult.

word:greek-nt:G2042.explanation: Erethizo means to stir up or provoke.

word:greek-nt:G2110.explanation: Euergetēs means a benefactor, a person who does good for others.

word:greek-nt:G2129.explanation: Eulogia means blessing. It can also mean praise or adulation, including flattering speech. It can also refer to a generous gift.

word:greek-nt:G2165.explanation: Euphrainō means to celebrate. It can also mean to be merry, as when a lost son is found and people celebrate.

word:greek-nt:G2226.explanation: Zōon means an animal. It can also mean a living creature, as in the creatures around the throne.

word:greek-nt:G2284.explanation: Thambeō means to amaze or to be amazed, describing a strong astonishment that can come close to terror.

word:greek-nt:G2323.explanation: Therapeuō means to heal. It describes healing sick people and those with various diseases.

word:greek-nt:G2473.explanation: Isopsychos means like-minded, sharing the same mind or spirit.

word:greek-nt:G2491.explanation: Iōannēs is the personal name John. It can identify John the Baptist or John who was taken with Peter and James up a high mountain.

word:greek-nt:G2547.explanation: Kakeithen means from there or thence, and it can also mean afterward.

word:greek-nt:G2608.explanation: Katagraphō means to break down, crush, or break into pieces. It is used for breaking legs.

word:greek-nt:G2644.explanation: Katallassō means to reconcile. It describes enemies being reconciled to God, and it can describe a wife being reconciled to her husband.

word:greek-nt:G2701.explanation: This Greek New Testament word means “to run down” or “to rush down.” It describes movement downward or toward a lower place, with the second wording emphasizing sudden or forceful action. The word occurs only once in the Greek New Testament, at Acts 21:32. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is active movement downward rather than simply being present or standing in a place.

word:greek-nt:G2806.explanation: Klaō means to break in pieces. It can specifically describe breaking bread.

word:greek-nt:G2932.explanation: Ktaomai means to acquire or purchase something. It can also mean to possess something.

word:greek-nt:G2987.explanation: This word means “brightness,” referring to a shining quality or visible radiance. It is a noun describing the brilliance that comes from something bright or luminous. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 26:13. Its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but the central idea remains the same: an intense, noticeable light or splendor. The word therefore points to brightness as something seen, rather than to a command, action, or inward attitude.

word:greek-nt:G3113.explanation: Makrothen means from a distance or afar.

word:greek-nt:G3395.explanation: Migma means a mixture, such as myrrh and aloes brought together.

word:greek-nt:G3412.explanation: Mitylene is the capital of the island of Lesbos.

word:greek-nt:G3625.explanation: It refers to the inhabited world, the humanly populated realm.

word:greek-nt:G3650.explanation: Holos means all. It can also mean the whole or something in its entirety, rather than only part of it.

word:greek-nt:G3669.explanation: Homoiosis means likeness or resemblance, describing people as made in the image of God.

word:greek-nt:G3737.explanation: Orphanos means an orphan. It can also describe someone who is fatherless.

word:greek-nt:G3782.explanation: Opheilē means a debt—something owed. It can also mean what is due, including respect, honor, or affection owed to another.

word:greek-nt:G3904.explanation: Paraskeue means the day of preparation, the day before the Sabbath.

word:greek-nt:G3948.explanation: This word refers to sharp disagreement or stirring up—an intense kind of provocation or contention. It can describe a conflict between people, but its sense also points to activity that arouses or stimulates a response. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, in Acts 15:39 and Hebrews 10:24. The surrounding verse determines whether the emphasis is on hostile disagreement or on provoking a needed response. Its central idea is something forceful that moves people toward strong reaction or action.

word:greek-nt:G4031.explanation: This word describes being “in control of” something or being “secure.” It points to a condition of control, stability, or safety rather than uncertainty or danger. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 27:16, and is rendered “secure.” Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding context, but its basic meaning is being firmly safe or under control.

word:greek-nt:G4112.explanation: This word describes something “made up”—something fabricated rather than genuinely true. It is used only once in the Greek New Testament, in 2 Peter 2:3. Its basic sense points to claims or statements that have been created or shaped falsely, rather than arising from truth. The surrounding verse determines exactly what is being described, but the word itself centers on the idea of something invented or fabricated.

word:greek-nt:G4237.explanation: Prasia means a group or company formed into divisions, like garden beds. It can describe a group seated in ranks by hundreds and fifties.

word:greek-nt:G4325.explanation: To spend extra means to use or pay more than what has already been provided or expected. This word expresses additional expenditure rather than the initial cost itself. It is a verb, so it describes the act of adding further expense. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Luke 10:35. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is the action or willingness to spend more.

word:greek-nt:G4350.explanation: Proskopto means to stumble or strike against something.

word:greek-nt:G4369.explanation: Prostithemi means to add or put something to something else.

word:greek-nt:G4413.explanation: Prōton means first or before, marking what comes earlier in time or order. It can also describe the foremost position.

word:greek-nt:G4695.explanation: Spiloō means to defile or stain.

word:greek-nt:G4776.explanation: Synkathizo means to sit down together or to sit down with someone else.

word:greek-nt:G4798.explanation: This word means “to associate with”—to connect or keep company with someone or something. It expresses an act of relating rather than naming a person, place, or object. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in John 4:9, so its normal meaning is represented by a single recorded use in that corpus. The surrounding verse and passage are needed to explain its particular force there.

word:greek-nt:G4800.explanation: Syzaō means to live together with.

word:greek-nt:G4875.explanation: This word means “to find rest together” or “to rest with.” It describes sharing rest with another person, rather than resting alone, and functions as an action word in a sentence. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Romans 15:32. The single occurrence means its fuller force is best understood from that passage’s surrounding words, though the basic idea remains resting together or finding mutual rest.

word:greek-nt:G4956.explanation: This word describes something commendatory or recommended—something presented favorably or offered as worthy of approval. It functions as a descriptive term rather than naming a person, object, or action by itself. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Corinthians 3:1. The surrounding verse determines exactly what is being commended or recommended there, but the word’s central idea is favorable presentation or approval.

word:greek-nt:G5043.explanation: Teknon means a child or children.

word:greek-nt:G5168.explanation: This word refers to an “eye” or a “hole.” It names a small opening or the eye itself, depending on how it is used in a sentence. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Mark 10:25. The word’s basic sense is therefore concise: it identifies an eye or a hole rather than expressing an action, quality, or relationship. The surrounding verse determines which of these related senses is intended there.

word:greek-nt:G5186.explanation: Typhloō means to make blind, physically or mentally.

word:greek-nt:G5249.explanation: Hyperperissōs means superabundantly, beyond measure, or exceedingly.

word:greek-nt:G5270.explanation: Hypokato means under, underneath, or below.

word:greek-nt:G5357.explanation: Phiale means a shallow, flat bowl. The golden bowls hold incense associated with the prayers of the saints.

word:greek-nt:G5436.explanation: Phygelus is a personal name, referring to an individual rather than expressing a general idea, action, or quality. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Timothy 1:15. The name itself identifies the person; the surrounding verse and passage are needed to understand what is said about him there. Scripture preserves this name as part of the historical record of the people mentioned in the New Testament.

word:greek-nt:G5494.explanation: Cheimōn means winter. It can also mean a storm or tempest.

word:greek-nt:G5519.explanation: Choiros means a swine, hog, or sow, rendered in English as pig or pigs.

word:greek-nt:G5520.explanation: Cholao means to be angry with someone.

word:greek-nt:G5555.explanation: Chrysolithos means chrysolite, a gem with a bright yellow color.

word:greek-nt:G6028.explanation: Ἐξεθαύμαζον means to be amazed or to wonder, as shown by their marveling greatly.

word:greek-nt:G6064.explanation: This word refers to a household or to a servant in a household. It describes someone connected with the domestic household setting, with particular emphasis on household service rather than a general kind of service. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Matthew 24:45. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning centers on household service and responsibility.
